claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a predominantly single-phase fcc matrix.
Additive manufacturing leaves local elemental inhomogeneities or minor segregation in this alloy.
Local elemental inhomogeneities promote a non-uniform Cr-Al-rich oxide scale during elevated-temperature exposure.
Oxidation of compositionally complex alloys can produce compositionally layered, locally differentiated oxide structures.
Local microsegregation directs preferential oxidation of Cr and Al.
Preferential oxidation produces protective oxide in some regions and thin or discontinuous oxide in others.
The resulting non-uniform oxide scale is incomplete or poorly adherent.
Thermal stress and thermal-expansion mismatch cause the non-uniform scale to spall.
Oxide-scale spallation initiates microcracks and accelerates degradation of the fcc matrix.
A reducing atmosphere suppresses sustained oxide formation and thereby mitigates microcracking and degradation.
Oxidizing exposure will produce more scale spallation, microcracks, mass change or loss, and surface damage than reducing exposure.
Identical samples can be compared under oxidizing and reducing or inert atmospheres while geometry and thermal history are held constant.
Scale continuity, thickness, adherence, oxide phases, mass change, and microcrack density can be measured using microscopy, XRD, weighing, and image analysis.
The hypothesis is restricted to elevated temperatures and gas compositions that clearly establish oxidizing and reducing regimes.
The quantitative influence of local compositional heterogeneity on scale formation and spallation is not established.
Failure to observe significantly greater spallation, microcracking, or mass loss under oxidizing exposure than under reducing exposure would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis, mechanism, and baseline say significant oxide-scale formation is absent or suppressed under reducing conditions, whereas the predicted outcome says the reducing environment will 'preserve scale.' It is unclear whether an oxide scale is expected to exist in that control.
